content: The kelvin, denoted by the symbol K, is a fundamental unit of temperature measurement and one of the seven base units in the International System of Units (SI). The Kelvin scale is a thermodynamic or absolute temperature scale, where absolute zero, the theoretical point at which all thermal energy ceases, is defined as 0 K. This scale and its unit are named after the Northern Irish physicist and engineer William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin (1824–1907), who emphasized the necessity of an absolute thermometric scale. The kelvin is defined by two fixed points: absolute zero and the triple point of Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW). This definition establishes a precise relationship between the Kelvin scale and the Celsius scale. For example, the triple point of water is defined as 273.16 K, which corresponds to 0.01 °C. Temperatures in kelvin can be converted to other units using these fixed points. Historically, the Celsius scale once defined the boiling point of water at one standard atmosphere as exactly 100 °C. However, this definition has been refined, and the actual boiling point of water depends on specific conditions, such as pressure. For more details on the boiling point of water, reference is made to VSMOW in temperature measurement. When referring to the unit kelvin, it is always written in lowercase unless it begins a sentence. However, when discussing the Kelvin scale, the word Kelvin functions as an adjective and is capitalized. Until the 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1967–1968, the kelvin was referred to as a degree, similar to other temperature scales. It was distinguished by terms like degree Kelvin or degree absolute, with the symbol °K. The 13th CGPM officially changed the name to simply kelvin with the symbol K, eliminating the term degree. The kelvin symbol is always represented as a capital K in roman, non-italic typeface. This capitalization aligns with the SI convention of capitalizing symbols named after individuals and avoids confusion with the SI prefix kilo, which uses a lowercase k. In scientific and engineering contexts, variables like pressure (P) and the speed of light (c) are italicized, but the kelvin symbol remains upright. Unicode includes a special kelvin sign at U+212A, which resembles an uppercase K. Depending on the operating system, web browser, and font, the Unicode kelvin sign may appear slightly different from a standard uppercase K. If a computer does not support the Unicode kelvin sign, it may be decomposed into a regular uppercase K, making them visually identical. The kelvin is also widely used in measuring the color temperature of light sources. Color temperature is based on the principle that a black body radiator emits light whose color depends on its temperature. Black bodies with temperatures below approximately 4000 K appear reddish, while those above 7500 K appear bluish. This concept is critical in fields like photography and image projection, where a color temperature of around 5500 K is required to match daylight film emulsions. In astronomy, the classification of stars and their placement on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram are partly based on their surface temperatures. For instance, the Sun has an effective photosphere temperature of 5778 K. Historically, the Kelvin scale has undergone significant milestones. In 1848, Lord Kelvin (William Thomson) proposed the need for an absolute thermometric scale, where infinite cold (absolute zero) would be the null point, and the degree Celsius would serve as the unit increment. He calculated absolute zero to be equivalent to −273 °C based on air thermometers of the time. This absolute scale is now known as the Kelvin thermodynamic temperature scale. In 1967–1968, the 13th CGPM renamed the unit increment of thermodynamic temperature to kelvin (symbol K), replacing the term degree absolute (symbol °K). In 2005, the Comité International des Poids et Mesures (CIPM) affirmed that the definition of the Kelvin scale would refer to water with an isotopic composition precisely matching the nominal specification of VSMOW water for the purposes of defining the temperature of the triple point of water.
